title: Learning curves and variability
goals: Describe variability across repeated development runs
Avoid unsupported guarantees from a trend

prerequisite.prompt: What does validation loss add to training loss?
prerequisite.answer: Evidence about examples that did not fit the model parameters.

vocabulary: Performance plotted against training sample size
Another run under a recorded procedure
How much results differ between runs
Maximum minus minimum of observed values

blocks.text: A learning curve asks how performance changes as the amount of training evidence grows. Keep the validation protocol, model settings and metric comparable. Use subsets of training only; never add validation rows into the training subsets. Multiple repeats reveal sensitivity to sample selection or model randomness.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines learning curves and variability.

At training sizes 10, 20, 40, validation MAEs across three declared repeats are [7, 9, 8], [5, 7, 6], [4, 6, 5]. Means are 8, 6, 5 and ranges 2, 2, 2. Mean training MAEs are 1, 2, 3. Validation improves as training grows, while training error rises because fitting more varied examples can be harder.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Learning curves and variability at a glance
blocks.caption: The decreasing gap is encouraging in this experiment. It does not establish that doubling again will halve error. A range from three repeats is a descriptive spread, not a confidence interval or a guarantee that future results fall inside it. Repeated runs can share records and therefore are not independent studies.

blocks.label: Why can training error rise while validation error falls? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Record the actual subset identifiers and seeds for every repeat. If the validation population changes at the same time as training size, label that as a different experiment rather than attributing the difference only to more training data.

Collect additional data because it addresses a known coverage need, not merely to enlarge a count. When the curve stops improving, inspect labels, features and task suitability. Keep the final test reserved while planning these changes.

blocks.label: Why is an observed range not a confidence interval?

workbook.title: Summarize repeats
workbook.prompt: Calculate the mean and range for the 20-row condition.

workbook.title: Read both curves
workbook.prompt: Why can training error rise while validation error falls?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: More varied training cases may be harder to fit exactly while giving a pattern that generalizes better.

workbook.title: Avoid extrapolation
workbook.prompt: Can the 40-row result guarantee a mean MAE of 2.5 at 80 rows?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. The observed trend does not establish a fixed proportional improvement.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: At sizes 12 and 24, validation errors are [6, 8, 7] and [4, 7, 7]. Calculate means/ranges and a careful comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Means 7 and 6; ranges 2 and 3. The larger condition improves the mean by 1 but has greater observed spread in these three repeats.

workbook.title: Explain the spread
workbook.prompt: Why is an observed range not a confidence interval?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It only describes the smallest and largest observed repeats; no coverage-probability calculation or independent-sampling argument was supplied.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on learning curves and variability. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Saved classroom project records for critique; no personal student dataset required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: What does validation loss add to training loss? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Read the opening and model the worked evidence. Ask students to identify learning curve in context.
Complete W 1 and W 2 with support: summarize repeats; read both curves. Require the evidence, not only the final response.
Read the visual row by row. Collect the guided explanation and compare reasoning in pairs. Connect each conclusion to the stated evidence.
Retrieve the distinction between learning curve and repeat. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Discuss the application and complete W 3: Can the 40-row result guarantee a mean MAE of 2.5 at 80 rows?
Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Assess these outcomes: Read training-size learning curves; Describe variability across repeated development runs. Record any support used.
Use W 5 and the exit response to assess limits. Give targeted feedback, then the fresh retry. Save evidence of independent understanding.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided response: More varied training cases may be harder to fit exactly while giving a pattern that generalizes better. Exit response: It only describes the smallest and largest observed repeats; no coverage-probability calculation or independent-sampling argument was supplied.
misconceptions: Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: Mean(5+7+6)/3=6; range 7-5=2.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
It only describes the smallest and largest observed repeats; no coverage-probability calculation or independent-sampling argument was supplied.
The new case can be copied from the example

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Means 7 and 6; ranges 2 and 3. The larger condition improves the mean by 1 but has greater observed spread in these three repeats.
teacher.assessment: For independent W 4, require: Means 7 and 6; ranges 2 and 3. The larger condition improves the mean by 1 but has greater observed spread in these three repeats. Fresh retry errors [3, 5, 7]: mean 5, range 4. Require the description to say three observed runs rather than a guaranteed future interval. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.
teacher.support: Provide a blank evidence table and allow a verbal explanation before writing. Highlight the given conditions without supplying the W 4 conclusion. Use learning curve and repeat in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.
teacher.next: Next week: Feature engineering. Carry forward the saved evidence and the distinction between development choices and justified claims.
